passages.title: Moses recalls the failed entry
passages.summary: Moses addresses Israel east of the Jordan. He recalls appointed judges, the scouts’ report, and the refusal to enter Canaan. The speech selects earlier events to teach the present generation. A remembered journey is not a new movement by the listeners.
passages.uncertainty: Moab is the speech setting. Other markers show recalled places or future instructions. Regions and traditional locations are approximate.

lds.text: Consider how your account of a past decision shapes what others learn from it.

passages.title: Neighboring lands and Sihon
passages.summary: Moses recalls travel near Edom, Moab, and Ammon. Israel must respect those territories. The speech then recounts war against Sihon. The account distinguishes lands that Israel must leave alone from a territory acquired through war. Its violence remains part of the story.
passages.uncertainty: Moab is the speech setting. Other markers show recalled places or future instructions. Regions and traditional locations are approximate.

lds.text: Consider the limits placed on territorial claims. Read the whole account rather than only its victory language.

passages.title: Og, eastern settlements, and Joshua
passages.summary: Moses recalls the defeat of Og and the allocation of eastern land. He encourages Joshua but cannot enter the land himself. The account joins military success with a leadership limit. An eastern inheritance still carries duties toward the other tribes.
passages.uncertainty: Moab is the speech setting. Other markers show recalled places or future instructions. Regions and traditional locations are approximate.

lds.text: Consider how receiving a benefit can leave continuing obligations to others.

passages.title: Remember the covenant
passages.summary: Moses urges obedience and warns against images. He recalls Horeb and sets apart three eastern refuge towns. The speech makes remembered experience a duty to future generations. The warnings concern covenant loyalty rather than a measured history of every event.
passages.uncertainty: Moab is the speech setting. Other markers show recalled places or future instructions. Regions and traditional locations are approximate.

lds.text: Consider how you can teach what you have learned without adding claims that the text does not make.

passages.title: The commandments recalled
passages.summary: Moses repeats the commandments and recalls Israel’s request for him to act as mediator. The Sabbath instruction remembers slavery in Egypt. Compare this account with Exodus 20. The Sabbath reasons differ even though the command concerns the same weekly rest.
passages.uncertainty: Moab is the speech setting. Other markers show recalled places or future instructions. Regions and traditional locations are approximate.

lds.text: Consider how the memory of slavery can shape rest and care for other people.

passages.title: Love, teach, and remember
passages.summary: Moses calls Israel to love the Lord and teach these words in daily life. He warns against forgetting after receiving a good land. The commands connect memory with ordinary places and repeated actions. Prosperity can make dependence on others easier to forget.
passages.uncertainty: Moab is the speech setting. Other markers show recalled places or future instructions. Regions and traditional locations are approximate.

lds.text: Come, Follow Me studies love for God and teaching the next generation. Consider one daily practice that supports remembrance.

passages.title: A chosen people and severe commands
passages.summary: The speech commands separation from surrounding worship and the destruction of named peoples. It also recalls God’s covenant with the ancestors. The chapter combines divine love with commands for collective violence. Those commands must not become permission for violence against people today.
passages.uncertainty: Moab is the speech setting. Other markers show recalled places or future instructions. Regions and traditional locations are approximate.

lds.text: Read covenant responsibilities beside the harm described in the chapter. Keep ancient commands distinct from present Church conduct.

passages.title: Remember in prosperity
passages.summary: Moses recalls wilderness hunger and manna. He warns that a prosperous people must not claim that its own strength supplied everything. The chapter links material success with memory and humility. Its account of wilderness testing belongs to the text’s religious explanation.
passages.uncertainty: Moab is the speech setting. Other markers show recalled places or future instructions. Regions and traditional locations are approximate.

lds.text: The Church lesson asks readers to remember God in comfort as well as hardship. Consider what gratitude changes in your conduct.

passages.title: The calf and intercession recalled
passages.summary: Moses denies that Israel receives the land because of its own righteousness. He recalls the golden calf, broken tablets, and his intercession. The speech opposes self-congratulation with a record of failure. Moses’s remembered prayers stress the community’s dependence on mercy.
passages.uncertainty: Moab is the speech setting. Other markers show recalled places or future instructions. Regions and traditional locations are approximate.

lds.text: Consider how honest memory can resist claims of moral superiority.

passages.title: New tablets and care for strangers
passages.summary: Moses recalls replacement tablets and the appointment of Levites. He calls Israel to love God and care for the stranger. The commands join worship with social responsibility. Love for the stranger draws on the memory of being strangers in Egypt.
passages.uncertainty: Moab is the speech setting. Other markers show recalled places or future instructions. Regions and traditional locations are approximate.

lds.text: Consider how memory of vulnerability can change your treatment of a newcomer.

passages.title: Teach the words and choose a path
passages.summary: Moses recalls Egypt and the judgment on Dathan and Abiram. He urges daily teaching and names Gerizim and Ebal for future blessings and curses. The speech uses remembered events and an anticipated ceremony to press a choice. Naming the mountains does not place the present assembly there.
passages.uncertainty: Moab is the speech setting. Other markers show recalled places or future instructions. Regions and traditional locations are approximate.

lds.text: Consider what habits help a family pass on its commitments.

passages.title: The chosen place of worship
passages.summary: The law requires worship at a place God will choose. It distinguishes sacrifices from ordinary meat eaten at home and forbids consuming blood. The chapter describes a central place without naming Jerusalem. Do not put a Jerusalem marker on the map as if this chapter named it.
passages.uncertainty: Moab is the speech setting. Other markers show recalled places or future instructions. Regions and traditional locations are approximate.

lds.text: Consider how shared worship can shape community life. Keep the text’s unnamed sanctuary distinct from a later identification.

passages.title: Tests of covenant loyalty
passages.summary: The law addresses a prophet, close relative, or town that urges worship of other gods. It prescribes severe punishments. The commands place loyalty above family and local ties. Their coercion belongs to an ancient legal setting and does not authorize present persecution.
passages.uncertainty: Moab is the speech setting. Other markers show recalled places or future instructions. Regions and traditional locations are approximate.

lds.text: Consider how to examine a religious claim carefully. Keep this ancient punishment system distinct from present conduct.

passages.title: Food, tithes, and shared provision
passages.summary: The law distinguishes permitted foods and directs the use of tithes. A third-year provision supports Levites, strangers, orphans, and widows. The chapter connects sacred identity with material care. Food rules and provision for vulnerable people have different functions within that system.
passages.uncertainty: Moab is the speech setting. Other markers show recalled places or future instructions. Regions and traditional locations are approximate.

lds.text: Consider how your use of resources can include people who lack stable support.

passages.title: Release and an open hand
passages.summary: The law provides for debt release and the release of Hebrew slaves. It requires generosity toward people in need and gifts to people released from slavery. The instructions address economic dependence within an unequal society. They require support as well as release from an obligation.
passages.uncertainty: Moab is the speech setting. Other markers show recalled places or future instructions. Regions and traditional locations are approximate.

lds.text: Come, Follow Me studies a willing heart in helping people in need. Consider whether your help preserves their dignity.

passages.title: Festivals and fair judgment
passages.summary: The law describes Passover, weeks, and booths. It also commands judges to avoid partiality and bribery. The festivals include people who might otherwise remain outside a household’s celebration. Fair judgment is a public duty.
passages.uncertainty: Moab is the speech setting. Other markers show recalled places or future instructions. Regions and traditional locations are approximate.

lds.text: Consider how celebrations and decisions can include people with less influence.

passages.title: Judges and limits on kings
passages.summary: The law addresses prohibited worship, difficult cases, and a future king. The king must read the law and limit wealth, horses, and wives. Royal power remains subject to instruction. The king must not raise himself above his fellow Israelites.
passages.uncertainty: Moab is the speech setting. Other markers show recalled places or future instructions. Regions and traditional locations are approximate.

lds.text: Consider what prevents a leader from treating authority as personal privilege.

passages.title: Priests and a prophet like Moses
passages.summary: The law provides support for priests, rejects certain divination practices, and promises a prophet like Moses. It gives a test for a prophetic claim. The chapter distinguishes authorized instruction from prohibited practices. Later Christian and LDS texts apply the promised prophet to Jesus Christ.
passages.uncertainty: Moab is the speech setting. Other markers show recalled places or future instructions. Regions and traditional locations are approximate.

lds.text: Come, Follow Me connects the prophet like Moses with Christ. Read that interpretation beside Acts 3 and 3 Nephi 20.

passages.title: Refuge, boundaries, and witnesses
passages.summary: The law establishes refuge for accidental killers, protects boundary markers, and requires multiple witnesses. False testimony receives a stated penalty. The procedures distinguish an accident from deliberate murder. An accusation alone cannot establish guilt in the stated system.
passages.uncertainty: Moab is the speech setting. Other markers show recalled places or future instructions. Regions and traditional locations are approximate.

lds.text: Consider why judgment needs witnesses and attention to circumstances.

passages.title: Rules for warfare
passages.summary: The law gives exemptions from military service and different instructions for distant and nearby cities. It limits destruction of fruit trees. The chapter contains both restraints and commands for collective killing. Those commands do not establish that each named conquest occurred.
passages.uncertainty: Moab is the speech setting. Other markers show recalled places or future instructions. Regions and traditional locations are approximate.

lds.text: Read the restraints and the violence together. Keep ancient war law distinct from present religious duty.

passages.title: Unsolved killing and household laws
passages.summary: The law addresses an unidentified killer, a captive woman, inheritance, a rebellious son, and burial after execution. The chapter brings public responsibility beside unequal household power and severe penalties. Its captive-marriage rules do not establish free consent.
passages.uncertainty: Moab is the speech setting. Other markers show recalled places or future instructions. Regions and traditional locations are approximate.

lds.text: Consider whose voice is absent from these laws. Keep the ancient penalties distinct from present family conduct.

passages.title: Neighborly care and sexual laws
passages.summary: The law requires help with lost animals and safe roofs. It also gives clothing rules and severe laws about marriage accusations and sexual acts. Practical care stands beside an unequal ancient sexual legal system. A failure to cry out must not become a modern test of consent.
passages.uncertainty: Moab is the speech setting. Other markers show recalled places or future instructions. Regions and traditional locations are approximate.

lds.text: Consider the duty to prevent foreseeable harm. Read the sexual laws within their ancient setting rather than using them to judge a survivor.

passages.title: Assembly, camp, and promises
passages.summary: The law restricts assembly membership, regulates camp cleanliness, and protects a person who escapes slavery from forced return. It also concerns interest and vows. The chapter contains both exclusion and protection. Read each rule rather than treating all outsiders as one category.
passages.uncertainty: Moab is the speech setting. Other markers show recalled places or future instructions. Regions and traditional locations are approximate.

lds.text: Consider the protection offered to a person escaping slavery. Keep ancient membership restrictions distinct from present human worth.

passages.title: Household changes and protection of the poor
passages.summary: The law concerns divorce and remarriage, loans, wages, testimony, and gleaning. It protects certain essential belongings from seizure. Daily economic rules can reduce harm to people with less power. The chapter remembers slavery as a reason for fair treatment.
passages.uncertainty: Moab is the speech setting. Other markers show recalled places or future instructions. Regions and traditional locations are approximate.

lds.text: Consider how prompt payment and leaving resources for others can turn compassion into action.

passages.title: Fair measures and family continuity
passages.summary: The law limits flogging, regulates marriage after a brother’s death, requires honest weights, and remembers Amalek’s attack. The chapter combines restraint, household continuity, commerce, and hostility. The marriage rule belongs to an ancient inheritance system.
passages.uncertainty: Moab is the speech setting. Other markers show recalled places or future instructions. Regions and traditional locations are approximate.

lds.text: Consider why a fair measure matters when another person cannot verify your claim.

passages.title: First produce and covenant declaration
passages.summary: The worshiper brings first produce and recounts the ancestors’ hardship, Egypt, and deliverance. A declaration accompanies the third-year tithe. The ritual connects possession of land with remembered dependence and shared provision. It turns a gift into a spoken account of identity.
passages.uncertainty: Moab is the speech setting. Other markers show recalled places or future instructions. Regions and traditional locations are approximate.

lds.text: Consider how giving can include an honest account of what you received from others.

passages.title: Instructions for Ebal and Gerizim
passages.summary: Moses and the elders give instructions for an altar, written law, and spoken curses after entry. Tribes receive roles on the two mountains. This chapter plans a future ceremony. Its curses name hidden wrongs and failures of justice as well as worship offenses.
passages.uncertainty: Moab is the speech setting. Other markers show recalled places or future instructions. Regions and traditional locations are approximate.

lds.text: Consider what a public promise requires when wrongdoing can remain hidden.

passages.title: Blessings and terrible curses
passages.summary: The speech lists blessings for obedience and curses for disobedience. It describes disease, military defeat, siege, hunger, and exile. The chapter expresses covenant consequences in severe terms. It cannot establish that a person’s present illness or suffering proves wrongdoing.
passages.uncertainty: Moab is the speech setting. Other markers show recalled places or future instructions. Regions and traditional locations are approximate.

lds.text: Read the whole warning with care. Avoid using its suffering language to assign blame to someone in distress.

passages.title: The covenant assembly
passages.summary: Moses addresses leaders, families, and strangers at the covenant gathering. He warns against hidden disloyalty and describes a devastated land. The commitment includes people present and people not present. The speech makes continuity across generations part of the covenant.
passages.uncertainty: Moab is the speech setting. Other markers show recalled places or future instructions. Regions and traditional locations are approximate.

lds.text: Come, Follow Me studies inward loyalty and shared covenant identity. Consider the effect of your choices on people who will follow you.

passages.title: Return and choose life
passages.summary: Moses describes return after scattering and calls the people to love and obey God. He presents the instruction as near and calls them to choose life. The chapter offers restoration beside warning. Its choice concerns love and conduct rather than a remote secret that cannot be reached.
passages.uncertainty: Moab is the speech setting. Other markers show recalled places or future instructions. Regions and traditional locations are approximate.

lds.text: The Church lesson compares these words with Lehi’s teaching about agency. Consider what choosing life requires in a daily decision.

passages.title: Joshua, the written law, and the song
passages.summary: Moses encourages Joshua, gives the written law to priests, and commands public readings. A song will serve as a witness against future unfaithfulness. Leadership, written instruction, and communal memory support continuity. The account also anticipates failure after Moses’s departure.
passages.uncertainty: Moab is the speech setting. Other markers show recalled places or future instructions. Regions and traditional locations are approximate.

lds.text: Consider how a community can preserve its commitments when a leader changes.

passages.title: The Song of Moses
passages.summary: The poem recounts God’s care, Israel’s neglect, judgment, and vindication. Moses then receives instructions to go up Mount Nebo. Poetry uses images that require interpretation. Deuteronomy 32 also has differences among surviving textual traditions that deserve separate study.
passages.uncertainty: Moab is the speech setting. Other markers show recalled places or future instructions. Regions and traditional locations are approximate.

lds.text: The older manual connects the rock image with Christ. Its race-related explanations require comparison with the Church’s current rejection of racial inferiority theories.

passages.title: Blessings for the tribes
passages.summary: Moses blesses the tribes before his departure. The poem names tribal identities and describes their hopes, duties, and regions. These ancestral names often designate communities, not the sons of Jacob standing before Moses. Simeon receives no separate blessing in this chapter.
passages.uncertainty: Moab is the speech setting. Other markers show recalled places or future instructions. Regions and traditional locations are approximate.

lds.text: Compare this poem with Genesis 49. Distinguish a tribal blessing from a secure date or a prediction independently verified by archaeology.

passages.title: Moses’s departure and Joshua’s leadership
passages.summary: Moses views the land from Nebo. The chapter narrates his death and an unknown burial place. Joshua receives the people’s obedience. The closing tribute honors Moses and confirms Joshua’s succession. The text does not identify a recoverable burial location.
passages.uncertainty: Moab is the speech setting. Other markers show recalled places or future instructions. Regions and traditional locations are approximate.

lds.text: LDS sources interpret Moses’s departure as translation, a change without ordinary death. Keep that interpretation distinct from this chapter’s stated account.

lds.text: Consider how shared worship can shape community life. Keep the text’s unnamed sanctuary distinct from a later identification.

events.title: Tests of covenant loyalty
events.summary: The law addresses a prophet, close relative, or town that urges worship of other gods. It prescribes severe punishments.
events.detail: The commands place loyalty above family and local ties. Their coercion belongs to an ancient legal setting and does not authorize present persecution.
events.uncertainty: Moab is the speech setting. Other markers show recalled places or future instructions. Regions and traditional locations are approximate.

lds.text: Consider how to examine a religious claim carefully. Keep this ancient punishment system distinct from present conduct.

events.title: Food, tithes, and shared provision
events.summary: The law distinguishes permitted foods and directs the use of tithes. A third-year provision supports Levites, strangers, orphans, and widows.
events.detail: The chapter connects sacred identity with material care. Food rules and provision for vulnerable people have different functions within that system.
events.uncertainty: Moab is the speech setting. Other markers show recalled places or future instructions. Regions and traditional locations are approximate.

lds.text: Consider how your use of resources can include people who lack stable support.

events.title: Release and an open hand
events.summary: The law provides for debt release and the release of Hebrew slaves. It requires generosity toward people in need and gifts to people released from slavery.
events.detail: The instructions address economic dependence within an unequal society. They require support as well as release from an obligation.
events.uncertainty: Moab is the speech setting. Other markers show recalled places or future instructions. Regions and traditional locations are approximate.

lds.text: Come, Follow Me studies a willing heart in helping people in need. Consider whether your help preserves their dignity.

events.title: Festivals and fair judgment
events.summary: The law describes Passover, weeks, and booths. It also commands judges to avoid partiality and bribery.
events.detail: The festivals include people who might otherwise remain outside a household’s celebration. Fair judgment is a public duty.
events.uncertainty: Moab is the speech setting. Other markers show recalled places or future instructions. Regions and traditional locations are approximate.

lds.text: Consider how celebrations and decisions can include people with less influence.

events.title: Judges and limits on kings
events.summary: The law addresses prohibited worship, difficult cases, and a future king. The king must read the law and limit wealth, horses, and wives.
events.detail: Royal power remains subject to instruction. The king must not raise himself above his fellow Israelites.
events.uncertainty: Moab is the speech setting. Other markers show recalled places or future instructions. Regions and traditional locations are approximate.

lds.text: Consider what prevents a leader from treating authority as personal privilege.

events.title: Priests and a prophet like Moses
events.summary: The law provides support for priests, rejects certain divination practices, and promises a prophet like Moses. It gives a test for a prophetic claim.
events.detail: The chapter distinguishes authorized instruction from prohibited practices. Later Christian and LDS texts apply the promised prophet to Jesus Christ.
events.uncertainty: Moab is the speech setting. Other markers show recalled places or future instructions. Regions and traditional locations are approximate.

lds.text: Come, Follow Me connects the prophet like Moses with Christ. Read that interpretation beside Acts 3 and 3 Nephi 20.

events.title: Refuge, boundaries, and witnesses
events.summary: The law establishes refuge for accidental killers, protects boundary markers, and requires multiple witnesses. False testimony receives a stated penalty.
events.detail: The procedures distinguish an accident from deliberate murder. An accusation alone cannot establish guilt in the stated system.
events.uncertainty: Moab is the speech setting. Other markers show recalled places or future instructions. Regions and traditional locations are approximate.

lds.text: Consider why judgment needs witnesses and attention to circumstances.

events.title: Rules for warfare
events.summary: The law gives exemptions from military service and different instructions for distant and nearby cities. It limits destruction of fruit trees.
events.detail: The chapter contains both restraints and commands for collective killing. Those commands do not establish that each named conquest occurred.
events.uncertainty: Moab is the speech setting. Other markers show recalled places or future instructions. Regions and traditional locations are approximate.

lds.text: Read the restraints and the violence together. Keep ancient war law distinct from present religious duty.

events.title: Unsolved killing and household laws
events.summary: The law addresses an unidentified killer, a captive woman, inheritance, a rebellious son, and burial after execution.
events.detail: The chapter brings public responsibility beside unequal household power and severe penalties. Its captive-marriage rules do not establish free consent.
events.uncertainty: Moab is the speech setting. Other markers show recalled places or future instructions. Regions and traditional locations are approximate.

lds.text: Consider whose voice is absent from these laws. Keep the ancient penalties distinct from present family conduct.

events.title: Neighborly care and sexual laws
events.summary: The law requires help with lost animals and safe roofs. It also gives clothing rules and severe laws about marriage accusations and sexual acts.
events.detail: Practical care stands beside an unequal ancient sexual legal system. A failure to cry out must not become a modern test of consent.
events.uncertainty: Moab is the speech setting. Other markers show recalled places or future instructions. Regions and traditional locations are approximate.

lds.text: Consider the duty to prevent foreseeable harm. Read the sexual laws within their ancient setting rather than using them to judge a survivor.

events.title: Assembly, camp, and promises
events.summary: The law restricts assembly membership, regulates camp cleanliness, and protects a person who escapes slavery from forced return. It also concerns interest and vows.
events.detail: The chapter contains both exclusion and protection. Read each rule rather than treating all outsiders as one category.
events.uncertainty: Moab is the speech setting. Other markers show recalled places or future instructions. Regions and traditional locations are approximate.

lds.text: Consider the protection offered to a person escaping slavery. Keep ancient membership restrictions distinct from present human worth.

events.title: Household changes and protection of the poor
events.summary: The law concerns divorce and remarriage, loans, wages, testimony, and gleaning. It protects certain essential belongings from seizure.
events.detail: Daily economic rules can reduce harm to people with less power. The chapter remembers slavery as a reason for fair treatment.
events.uncertainty: Moab is the speech setting. Other markers show recalled places or future instructions. Regions and traditional locations are approximate.

lds.text: Consider how prompt payment and leaving resources for others can turn compassion into action.

events.title: Fair measures and family continuity
events.summary: The law limits flogging, regulates marriage after a brother’s death, requires honest weights, and remembers Amalek’s attack.
events.detail: The chapter combines restraint, household continuity, commerce, and hostility. The marriage rule belongs to an ancient inheritance system.
events.uncertainty: Moab is the speech setting. Other markers show recalled places or future instructions. Regions and traditional locations are approximate.

lds.text: Consider why a fair measure matters when another person cannot verify your claim.

events.title: First produce and covenant declaration
events.summary: The worshiper brings first produce and recounts the ancestors’ hardship, Egypt, and deliverance. A declaration accompanies the third-year tithe.
events.detail: The ritual connects possession of land with remembered dependence and shared provision. It turns a gift into a spoken account of identity.
events.uncertainty: Moab is the speech setting. Other markers show recalled places or future instructions. Regions and traditional locations are approximate.

lds.text: Consider how giving can include an honest account of what you received from others.

events.title: Instructions for Ebal and Gerizim

events.detail: This chapter plans a future ceremony. Its curses name hidden wrongs and failures of justice as well as worship offenses.
events.uncertainty: Moab is the speech setting. Other markers show recalled places or future instructions. Regions and traditional locations are approximate.

lds.text: Consider what a public promise requires when wrongdoing can remain hidden.

events.title: Blessings and terrible curses
events.summary: The speech lists blessings for obedience and curses for disobedience. It describes disease, military defeat, siege, hunger, and exile.
events.detail: The chapter expresses covenant consequences in severe terms. It cannot establish that a person’s present illness or suffering proves wrongdoing.
events.uncertainty: Moab is the speech setting. Other markers show recalled places or future instructions. Regions and traditional locations are approximate.

lds.text: Read the whole warning with care. Avoid using its suffering language to assign blame to someone in distress.

events.title: The covenant assembly
events.summary: Moses addresses leaders, families, and strangers at the covenant gathering. He warns against hidden disloyalty and describes a devastated land.
events.detail: The commitment includes people present and people not present. The speech makes continuity across generations part of the covenant.
events.uncertainty: Moab is the speech setting. Other markers show recalled places or future instructions. Regions and traditional locations are approximate.

lds.text: Come, Follow Me studies inward loyalty and shared covenant identity. Consider the effect of your choices on people who will follow you.

events.title: Return and choose life
events.summary: Moses describes return after scattering and calls the people to love and obey God. He presents the instruction as near and calls them to choose life.
events.detail: The chapter offers restoration beside warning. Its choice concerns love and conduct rather than a remote secret that cannot be reached.
events.uncertainty: Moab is the speech setting. Other markers show recalled places or future instructions. Regions and traditional locations are approximate.

lds.text: The Church lesson compares these words with Lehi’s teaching about agency. Consider what choosing life requires in a daily decision.

events.title: Joshua, the written law, and the song

events.detail: Leadership, written instruction, and communal memory support continuity. The account also anticipates failure after Moses’s departure.
events.uncertainty: Moab is the speech setting. Other markers show recalled places or future instructions. Regions and traditional locations are approximate.

lds.text: Consider how a community can preserve its commitments when a leader changes.

events.title: The Song of Moses
events.summary: The poem recounts God’s care, Israel’s neglect, judgment, and vindication. Moses then receives instructions to go up Mount Nebo.
events.detail: Poetry uses images that require interpretation. Deuteronomy 32 also has differences among surviving textual traditions that deserve separate study.
events.uncertainty: Moab is the speech setting. Other markers show recalled places or future instructions. Regions and traditional locations are approximate.

lds.text: The older manual connects the rock image with Christ. Its race-related explanations require comparison with the Church’s current rejection of racial inferiority theories.

events.title: Blessings for the tribes
events.summary: Moses blesses the tribes before his departure. The poem names tribal identities and describes their hopes, duties, and regions.

events.uncertainty: Moab is the speech setting. Other markers show recalled places or future instructions. Regions and traditional locations are approximate.

lds.text: Compare this poem with Genesis 49. Distinguish a tribal blessing from a secure date or a prediction independently verified by archaeology.

events.uncertainty: Moab is the speech setting. Other markers show recalled places or future instructions. Regions and traditional locations are approximate.

textRoutes.title: Moses recalls the failed entry
textRoutes.summary: Moses addresses Israel east of the Jordan. He recalls appointed judges, the scouts’ report, and the refusal to enter Canaan.
textRoutes.detail: The speech selects earlier events to teach the present generation. A remembered journey is not a new movement by the listeners.
textRoutes.uncertainty: Moses recalls the Horeb-to-Kadesh journey in Deuteronomy 1. This is a retrospective, simplified line. It omits uncertain camps and does not show an excavated road.
